title: Create, compare, subtract
blurb: datetime, date and time objects: build them, compare them, subtract them. Subtracting two time objects fails.
code: dt2 = datetime.datetime(day=1, month=1, year=2011, hour=10, minute=10, second=10)

notes.2: datetime(year, month, day, hour, minute, second): year, month and day are required, the rest default to 0.
notes.3: Keyword arguments can be given in any order.
notes.4: datetime minus datetime gives a timedelta (2010 to 2011 has no leap day, so 365 days).
notes.5: Comparison operators work on datetime objects and return a bool.
notes.6: dt2 is later than dt1, so < is False.
notes.7: A date object keeps only year, month and day.
notes.9: date minus date also gives a timedelta (2015 is not a leap year).
notes.10: A time object keeps only hour, minute and second.
notes.13: Subtracting two time objects is not allowed: there is no date to measure a duration against.

title: timedelta arithmetic
blurb: Subtract two datetimes to get a timedelta, split it with divmod, and add it back to a datetime.

notes.2: from datetime import * brings datetime, date, time, timedelta straight into the namespace.
notes.3: The same moment, one year later.
notes.4: td is a timedelta: it stores days, seconds and microseconds (here 365 days).
notes.5: divmod(365, 30) = 12 whole months of 30 days and 5 days left over.
notes.6: divmod(365, 7) = 52 whole weeks and 1 day left over.
notes.7: timedelta(31) means 31 days (days is the first parameter).
notes.8: A normal datetime to add to.
notes.9: datetime + timedelta gives a new datetime, 31 days later.
notes.10: Adding the 365 day timedelta moves the date one year ahead.

title: strftime and strptime
blurb: strftime turns a datetime into text, strptime turns text into a datetime. Both use the same control characters.

notes.3: %d zero-padded day, %B month name, %A day name, %Y 4-digit year, %H %M %S hours, minutes, seconds.
notes.4: %-d (no zero), %b short month, %a short day, %y 2-digit year. The minus flag works on Linux and macOS, not on Windows.
notes.5: A plain str: it knows nothing about dates yet.
notes.6: strptime reads the text using the same control characters and builds a datetime. The format must match the text exactly.
notes.7: print shows the datetime in ISO style.

title: time module: epoch and struct_time
blurb: Seconds since 1 Jan 1970 (the epoch) can be turned into a struct_time and back into text.

notes.2: Second 0 of the epoch is 1 Jan 1970, 00:00:00 UTC (a Thursday: tm_wday 3, Monday is 0).
notes.3: time.time() returns a float like this: seconds elapsed since the epoch.
notes.4: gmtime gives UTC fields, localtime gives your own time zone. Both return a struct_time.
notes.5: A struct_time is a named tuple: read a part by name.
notes.6: tm_mday is the day of the month.
notes.7: tm_hour is the hour on a 24 hour clock (UTC here).
notes.8: time.strftime formats a struct_time with the same control characters.

title: calendar functions
blurb: Leap years, weekdays and month lengths from the calendar module.

notes.2: 2024 is divisible by 4 and not a century year, so it is a leap year.
notes.3: Leap years from 2000 up to but not including 2022: 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020 = 6.
notes.4: weekday returns 0 for Monday ... 6 for Sunday. 1 Jan 2000 was a Saturday = 5.
notes.6: monthrange gives (weekday of the 1st, number of days). 1 Mar 2022 was a Tuesday (shown as calendar.TUESDAY, which equals 1), and the month has 31 days.
notes.7: month_name is indexed 1 to 12 (index 0 is an empty string).
